security_spec.violation_condition: On RV32 with Sv32p34 (34-bit physical addresses), the kernel configures a TOR PMP entry whose pmpaddr[i] would need the value 0x1_0000_0000 (34-bit, i.e., XLEN=32 shifted: 2^34 >> 2 = 2^32) to encompass the top of physical memory, but pmpaddr is only XLEN bits wide, so the maximum representable endpoint is 2^(XLEN+2)-4. Any kernel PMP setup code that iteratively chains TOR entries to cover 'all memory up to the end of DRAM' will silently leave the uppermost 4 bytes unprotected.
security_spec.summary: TOR PMP entries cannot address 2^(XLEN+2) as a range endpoint, so on RV32 with 34-bit PA the uppermost 4 bytes of physical memory cannot be covered by a TOR region; kernel PMP init code that assumes TOR chains can span the entire physical address space creates a 4-byte hole at the top of DRAM accessible to less-privileged modes

findings.finding: Only PMP setup in the kernel is a single NAPOT entry with pmpaddr0=-1 covering all memory; no TOR-based PMP configuration exists. The RV32 pmpaddr overflow vulnerability pattern (iterative TOR chaining where the top entry's pmpaddr would exceed XLEN bits) is not applicable because TOR mode is never used. PMP_A_TOR is defined in csr.h but has zero callers in the entire kernel tree.
findings.snippet:
li a0, -1
csrw CSR_PMPADDR0, a0
li a0, (PMP_A_NAPOT | PMP_R | PMP_W | PMP_X)
csrw CSR_PMPCFG0, a0
